title: South Korean Dramas Win Globally, but Profits Flow to Netflix — Federation of Korean Industries Urges Support for Korean OTT Platforms' Overseas Expansion - BigGo Finance

 Add preferred source South Korea's Federation of Korean Industries (FKI) convened the fourth Service Industry Competitiveness Committee meeting on the 18th at FKI Tower in Yeouido, Seoul, inviting South Korea's Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Choi Hwi-young to discuss structural problems in the K-content industry. Cho Young-shin, a professor at Dongguk University, noted that South Korea's content industry revenue hit a record 161 trillion won (approximately $121.1 billion) last year, but drama production fell from 141 titles in 2022 to about 100 in 2024. Season 1 of "Squid Game" generated roughly 1.0546 trillion won (approximately $793.0 million) in economic value, yet South Korean production companies earned only 2 billion to 4 billion won (approximately $1.5 million to $3.0 million). The FKI recommended 20 policy measures to the government, including support for South Korean OTT platforms' overseas expansion, expanding production support to more than 100 billion won (approximately $75.2 million), and introducing tax credits for game and music production costs. Key Elements 
 Federation of Korean Industries Choi Hwi-young Cho Young-shin Netflix Squid Game Viu iQIYI CJ ENM HYBE South Korea's Ministry of Culture Sports and Tourism South Korean dramas are winning over audiences worldwide, but the share that South Korean production companies actually take home remains negligible. Critics say that because intellectual property (IP) and distribution networks have been handed over to overseas platforms, ancillary revenue is flowing overseas in its entirety. South Korea's Federation of Korean Industries (FKI) convened the fourth Service Industry Competitiveness Committee meeting on the 18th at FKI Tower in Yeouido, Seoul, inviting South Korea's Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Choi Hwi-young to address these issues.
 Cho Young-shin, a professor at Dongguk University, who delivered the keynote presentation, diagnosed that while South Korea's content industry continues to grow on the surface, its production base is actually weakening. South Korea's content industry revenue reached a record 161 trillion won (approximately $121.1 billion) last year, with exports of $14.9 billion (about 19.8 trillion won). In contrast, drama production fell from 141 titles in 2022 to about 100 in 2024. In the first half of last year, Netflix accounted for 88% of new Korean series orders placed by global OTT platforms.
 Professor Cho identified ownership of distribution networks and IP as the reason for the diverging fortunes across sectors. Games, music, and webtoons saw revenue rise because South Korean operators hold distribution and IP, while film and broadcast/video content shrank as global OTT platforms took over those functions.
 The most representative case is Netflix's "Squid Game." Season 1 generated economic value of about 1.0546 trillion won (approximately $793.0 million) by Netflix's own estimate, but South Korean production companies earned only 2 billion to 4 billion won (approximately $1.5 million to $3.0 million), according to estimates by the National Assembly's Culture, Sports and Tourism Committee. Ancillary revenue from IP, including games, experiential attractions, and character merchandise, also accrued to Netflix as the IP holder.
 Professor Cho proposed overseas expansion by South Korean OTT platforms as the solution. Under the model of selling rights to overseas platforms, producers receive only one-off licensing fees and struggle to secure subscribers, usage data, and pricing power. By contrast, Hong Kong OTT platform Viu leveraged Korean dramas to more than triple its paid subscribers from 5.3 million in 2020 to 16.8 million last year and swing to profit. China's iQIYI likewise expanded its supply of Korean titles by 30% after Korean dramas accounted for 38% of total drama viewing time. This is evidence that demand for K-content can be sufficiently secured on platforms other than Netflix.
 "K-OTT platforms must secure overseas subscribers directly so that the revenue returns to expand South Korean content production and feed the production ecosystem, completing a virtuous cycle," Professor Cho stressed.
 To support this, the FKI recommended 20 policy measures to the government. The core proposals include expanding production support for securing IP by South Korean OTT platforms and producers to more than 100 billion won (approximately $75.2 million) over the medium to long term and more than 4 billion won (approximately $3.0 million) per title, and creating funds linked to private capital. The measures also include granting capital gains tax exemptions to investors in content policy funds and raising the Korea Content Completion Guarantee limit for large-scale projects from the current 5 billion won (approximately $3.8 million) to as much as 30 billion won (approximately $22.6 million).
 Calls for expanded tax support were also made. The FKI asked that game and music content production costs be newly included as eligible for tax credits, that tax benefits for content investors be strengthened, and that the Service Industry Development Framework Act be enacted. The game and music industries accounted for 73.2% of total content exports in 2024, but the current tax credit system is concentrated on video content.
 Category Key Details 
 Expanded production support More than 100 billion won (approximately $75.2 million) over the medium to long term, more than 4 billion won (approximately $3.0 million) per title 
 Guarantee limit Korea Content Completion Guarantee raised from 5 billion won (approximately $3.8 million) to as much as 30 billion won (approximately $22.6 million) 
 Tax New tax credits for game and music production costs, benefits for content investors 
 Funds Content policy funds linked to private capital, capital gains tax exemption 
 Legislation Enactment of the Service Industry Development Framework Act 
 Note: Key items among the 20 policy measures recommended to the government by the Federation of Korean Industries
 Huh Min-hoi, chairman of the FKI's Service Industry Competitiveness Committee, said, "Investment in the cultural industry is an investment that nurtures the entire K-lifestyle ecosystem," adding, "Institutional support from the government is needed so that the interest in South Korea created by content translates into results for our economy." The meeting was attended by about 20 executives from cultural and service industry companies, including Korean Air, Lotte Department Store, CJ ENM, and HYBE, as well as Chairman Huh.
 Minister Choi said, "K-culture is the third-largest export industry after semiconductors and automobiles," and pledged, "We will strengthen policy finance and tax support so that global interest can lead to corporate growth and expanded creation and investment."
 The discussion is significant in that it directly addressed the structural limitation that the global popularity of K-content does not translate into added value for South Korean industry. Concerns are raised that, with heavy reliance on orders from global platforms such as Netflix, if South Korean OTT platforms fail to secure self-sustaining revenue bases overseas, the decline in production volume and talent outflow could continue. Conversely, analysts say that if Korean platforms expand their overseas subscriber bases, a virtuous-cycle model that moves beyond one-off, licensing-fee-centered revenue structures to accumulate IP and data becomes possible. However, some observers note that, given Netflix's firmly established position in the South Korean market, it will not be easy for South Korean OTT platforms to secure meaningful subscriber numbers overseas in the short term.
